draft.title: Scale and maps
card: A map scale such as 1:50,000 means 1 unit on the map is 50,000 of the same unit in real life. So 1 cm on the map is 50,000 cm, which is 500 m on the ground.
To find a real distance, measure the map distance and multiply by the second number in the scale. Then change the units to something sensible.
Useful changes: 100 cm \(=\) 1 m, 1000 m \(=\) 1 km, and 100,000 cm \(=\) 1 km. So on a 1:50,000 map, 2 cm on the map is 100,000 cm, which is 1 km.
To go from real to map, change the real distance to cm, then divide by the scale number. On a 1:50,000 map, 3 km is 300,000 cm. \(300{,}000 \div 50{,}000 = 6\) cm on the map.
draft.remember: Map to real: multiply by the scale number. Real to map: change to cm, then divide by the scale number.

a.q: A walking track is 3 km long in real life. How long is it on a 1:50,000 map?
a.why: 3 km is 300,000 cm. \(300{,}000 \div 50{,}000 = 6\) cm. The option 60 cm comes from changing 3 km to only 30,000 cm, a unit mistake. The option 150 cm comes from multiplying instead of dividing.
a.clue: Change km to cm first, then divide by 50,000.

b.q: On a 1:25,000 map, a campsite and a lake are 7.2 cm apart. How far apart are they in real life?
b.why: \(7.2 \times 25{,}000 = 180{,}000\) cm. Dividing by 100,000 gives 1.8 km. The option 18 km comes from dividing by 10,000, which mixes up the cm to km change.
b.clue: Multiply by 25,000, then use 100,000 cm \(=\) 1 km.

problems.detail: The why for (a) is wrong about the distractors. Changing 3 km to 30,000 cm gives 30,000 ÷ 50,000 = 0.6 cm, not 60 cm. 60 cm comes from using 3,000,000 cm, one zero too many. Also, multiplying gives 3 × 50,000, which is not 150 cm, so the 150 cm explanation does not hold either.
Question a is the card's own worked example word for word: 3 km on a 1:50,000 map is 6 cm. Students can answer it from memory without applying the method. Use a different distance or scale.

a.q: A walking track is 2 km long in real life. How long is it on a 1:40,000 map?
a.why: 2 km is 200,000 cm, and \(200{,}000 \div 40{,}000 = 5\) cm. The option 0.05 cm comes from stopping at metres: \(2000 \div 40{,}000 = 0.05\). The option 50 cm comes from writing 2 km as 2,000,000 cm, one zero too many.
a.clue: Change km all the way to cm before you divide.

b.why: \(7.2 \times 25{,}000 = 180{,}000\) cm. Dividing by 100,000 gives 1.8 km. The option 18 km comes from dividing by 10,000, which mixes up the cm to km change.
b.clue: Multiply by 25,000, then use 100,000 cm \(=\) 1 km.
